primary_text_note: scripts/_retrofc/_texts/frankenstein.txt — Gutenberg #84, 1831 text, 4 letters + 24 continuous chapters. The 1831 Introduction is NOT in the file, so the two Introduction quotations in L1 were checked against the known wording of that Introduction rather than against this file.
spec_verified: Component 2 (1ET0/02): 80 marks, 2 hours 15 minutes, closed book. Section A 19th-century novel is a two part question — part (a) close language analysis of a printed extract of about 400 words (20 marks, AO2), part (b) an essay on the whole text (20 marks, AO1). AO3 and AO4 are not assessed on this section, and no SPaG marks are awarded on this paper.

findings.claim: “For Edexcel 1ET0 Component 2, Section A … Part (a) … (AO1 + AO2). Part (b) … (AO1 + AO2).”
findings.truth: Part (a) is 20 marks for AO2 only (close analysis of the printed extract). Part (b) is 20 marks for AO1 only (a critical whole-text response). Giving both parts “AO1 + AO2” tells a student to write for methods in part (b), which earns nothing there. “Edexcel 1ET0” and “Component 2, Section A” are also banned strings.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md, Component 2 overview (paper code 1ET0/02): Section A 19th-century novel is a two part question, part 1 close language analysis of an extract of about 400 words, part 2 an essay on the whole text; “Assessment Objectives covered are AO1 and AO2”. Section A carries 20 marks per part (1a–7a all AO2, 1b–7b all AO1).

findings.claim: “In the Edexcel exam, context is not assessed through a separate assessment objective — but it significantly strengthens your AO1 response.”
findings.truth: True only for the 19th-century novel question. AO3 is assessed on the Shakespeare part (b), on the post-1914 text and on the anthology poetry comparison. Read as written, the tip would cost marks on those questions. Scoped to this section.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md: Component 1 Section A “AO1, AO2 and AO3”; Section B “AO1, AO3 and AO4”; Component 2 Section B Part 1 poems compared for language, form, structure (AO2) and “the contexts in which the poems were written (AO3)”; Component 2 Section A “AO1 and AO2” only.

findings.claim: “It was only in the 1831 revised edition that Shelley was openly credited as the author.”
findings.truth: The 1818 first edition was anonymous, but the second edition of 1823 (two volumes, Whittaker, seen through the press by William Godwin while Mary Shelley was in Italy) carried “Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley” on the title page. 1831 was the revised one-volume edition with her Introduction, not the first to name her.
findings.evidence: Standard bibliographic record of the three lifetime editions (1818 anonymous, 1823 named, 1831 revised with Introduction). The unit already treats 1831 correctly as the edition with an Introduction (not a preface).

findings.claim: All 48 practice questions in the unit are typed “20 marks — Extract Analysis”.
findings.truth: 31 of them print no extract and ask for a whole-novel argument (“How does Shelley present … in the novel as a whole?”). Those are part (b), the whole-text essay. Relabelled “20 marks — Whole-Text Essay”, matching the label already used on the sister Edexcel novel units. The 17 genuine extract tasks keep the old label.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md, Component 2 overview: “Section A – 19th-century novel: a two part question, with the first part focussed on an extract of approximately 400 words. The second part is an essay question exploring the whole text.”

findings.claim: Chapter citations on the printed extracts: L2 “Volume 1, Chapter 4” and L3 “Volume 1, Chapter 5” for the same chapter; L4 and L8 “Volume 2, Chapter 7” for two different chapters; L5 “Volume 2, Chapter 9”.
findings.truth: In the 1831 text the unit works from, the creation scene is Chapter 5 (L2 and L3 contradict each other about it, and “Volume 1, Chapter 5” exists in no edition). “I ought to be thy Adam” is Chapter 10. “I am malicious because I am miserable” is Chapter 17, so L4 and L8 gave one label to two different chapters. The “Beware” speech is Chapter 20, not Volume 2 Chapter 9. All five now cite the continuous 1831 chapter number.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/_texts/frankenstein.txt (Gutenberg #84, 1831 text, 24 continuous chapters): creation scene opens Chapter 5 (line 1523); “I ought to be thy Adam” line 3055 = Chapter 10; “I am malicious because I am miserable” line 4637 = Chapter 17; “the wiliness of a snake” line 5439 = Chapter 20.

findings.claim: Flashcard: “Which Satan echo shows the Creature embracing an avenger role?” → “‘Evil, be thou my good.’”, and the same phrase inside the L4 question 5 mark scheme.
findings.truth: “Evil, be thou my good” is Milton (Paradise Lost IV.110), not Shelley. The Creature’s line is “Evil thenceforth became my good.” In a closed-book exam a memorised flashcard is written out as a quotation, so this hands the student a line from another text.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/_texts/frankenstein.txt line 7280 (Chapter 24): “Evil thenceforth became my good.” No occurrence of “be thou my good” anywhere in the novel. The lesson body attributes the phrase to Milton correctly; only the flashcard and the mark scheme present it as the Creature’s.

findings.claim: Question 1 extract: “… would tear me to pieces and triumph; shall I respect man when he condemns me?”
findings.truth: Those two clauses are about four sentences apart in the novel. Presented as a continuous printed extract, it teaches a quotation that does not exist in that form. An ellipsis now marks the cut.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/_texts/frankenstein.txt lines 4638–4643 (Chapter 17): “… would tear me to pieces and triumph; remember that, and tell me why I should pity man more than he pities me? You would not call it murder … Shall I respect man when he condemns me?”

findings.claim: “He swears to pursue the Creature ‘until he or I shall perish in mortal combat.’” — repeated as a flashcard answer.
findings.truth: The novel reads “mortal conflict”. “Combat” does appear in the novel, but in Victor’s Chapter 10 challenge, not in the oath.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/_texts/frankenstein.txt line 6651 (Chapter 24): “… until he or I shall perish in mortal conflict.”

findings.claim: Printed extract “from the Creature’s final speech”: “I, the miserable and the abandoned, am an abortion, an anomaly, a blot upon the earth, from which all men fled and whom all men disowned.” Also quoted in the lesson body as “… am an abortion, am a blot, am a wretch”, with word-level analysis of “blot” and “wretch”.
findings.truth: Fabricated. The word “anomaly” is nowhere in the novel. The real final-speech line is “I, the miserable and the abandoned, am an abortion, to be spurned at, and kicked, and trampled on.” The “blot upon the earth, from which all men fled and whom all men disowned” clause is real but comes from Chapter 13, eleven chapters earlier and in a different speech. The extract, the body quotation and the mark scheme are all corrected to the real Chapter 24 wording.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/_texts/frankenstein.txt lines 7329–7331 (Chapter 24) and line 3758 (Chapter 13: “Was I, then, a monster, a blot upon the earth, from which all men fled and whom all men disowned?”). Grep for “anomaly” returns nothing.

findings.claim: “Linking characters to themes is what lifts a response from Level 3 to Level 4.”
findings.truth: “Level 3” and “Level 4” are banned band names; the house ladder is used instead. Rewritten as “into the top bands”.
findings.evidence: Checker brief, banned strings: “Level 1”..“Level 9” band names.

findings.claim: “Elizabeth Lavenza is Victor’s cousin (adopted into the family) and later his wife.”
findings.truth: In the 1831 text the unit works from, Elizabeth is the orphaned daughter of a Milanese nobleman, taken in by Caroline; Victor says only that “we called each other familiarly by the name of cousin”. She is his cousin by blood only in the 1818 text. The rewrite is true of both editions.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/_texts/frankenstein.txt lines 776–811 (Chapter 1): “the daughter of a Milanese nobleman … Elizabeth Lavenza became the inmate of my parents’ house … We called each other familiarly by the name of cousin.”

findings.claim: “Purpose-driven analysis is what separates Level 3 from Level 4.”
findings.truth: Same banned band names as F10. Rewritten as “into the top bands”.
findings.evidence: Checker brief, banned strings: “Level 1”..“Level 9” band names.

findings.claim: “An extract-based task … (rewarding AO1 + AO2). A wider-text task … (also AO1 + AO2). Most GCSE literature exams are closed book … check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact mark weightings and timing.”
findings.truth: Same AO error as F1: part (a) is 20 marks AO2, part (b) is 20 marks AO1. The board is known, so the paper is closed book as a fact, not a maybe, and the marks should be stated rather than deferred to the student.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md, Component 2: “Closed book (texts are not allowed in the examination)”, 80 marks, 2 hours 15 minutes; Section A “Assessment Objectives covered are AO1 and AO2” with part 1 AO2 and part 2 AO1.

findings.claim: “For Part (a) of the Edexcel exam, you must analyse an extract focusing on _____ and/or structure (AO1 + AO2).”
findings.truth: Part (a) is AO2 only. The keyed answer (“language”, index 1) is correct; the AO label in the stem is not, and a knowledge check is exactly where a student memorises it.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md, Component 2 Section A: part 1 is close language analysis of the extract (AO2); part 2 is the whole-text essay (AO1).

findings.claim: Question 5 prints a passage from Shelley’s 1831 Introduction and labels it an extract task.
findings.truth: The real part (a) always prints a passage from the novel itself, never from the Introduction. The quotation is verbatim and the analysis is sound, so it is a useful context exercise, but it is not a rehearsal of the exam task. Not edited.

summary: 15 findings across all 8 lessons (8 HIGH, 6 MEDIUM, 1 LOW note); 54 edits. The exam frame is board-correct in outline — no 30-mark essay, no AQA AO split, no SPaG claim, no open-book claim — but the AO split inside the two-part question is wrong in three places (L1 body, L8 body, L8 knowledge check all give both parts “AO1 + AO2”), and “Level 3”/“Level 4” band names plus the “Edexcel 1ET0 Component 2, Section A” spec code would fail the validator. The worst content fault is L6: the Creature’s final-speech extract is fabricated (“anomaly” appears nowhere in the novel, and the “blot upon the earth” clause is spliced in from Chapter 13), with a mark scheme built on the invented wording; the same lesson misquotes Victor’s oath as “mortal combat” for “mortal conflict”. L4 teaches Milton’s “Evil, be thou my good” as a Frankenstein quotation on a memorisation flashcard. The AQA faults listed in the brief did not recur: tabula rasa is credited to Locke, galvanism is dated to the early nineteenth century, the “new Adam” line is quoted correctly and in full, 1831 is called an Introduction, and the plot order around the De Lacey beating is right.
